sources.title: How do you keep food safe during a power failure?
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
sources.supports: A refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours if unopened; a full stand-alone freezer holds temperature about 48 hours (24 if half full) with the door closed; a refrigerator's freezer compartment may not hold as long; group freezer packages together.
sources.notes: Short Q&A that points to the longer FSIS emergencies page. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

sources.title: What foods should I keep in my house for emergencies?
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
sources.supports: Keep nonperishable food and a 3-day supply of commercially bottled water per person (minimum 3 gallons); example foods; choose small cans so there are no leftovers needing refrigeration; include infant formula, pet food and special-diet foods; have a manual can opener; periodically use and refresh the supply.
sources.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. The first fetch returned only the page title; a second fetch with a render wait returned the full text.

sources.title: National Center for Home Food Preservation
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia
sources.supports: Describes itself as the source of current research-based recommendations for most methods of home food preservation, established with USDA funding to address food-safety concerns; sections on canning, pickling, fermenting, freezing, drying, curing and smoking, and storing.
sources.notes: Home page only. Used as the hub link. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

sources.title: Jerky
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (extracted from So Easy to Preserve, 6th ed.)
sources.supports: Jerky safety procedure: raw poultry generally not recommended; freeze pork and wild game 6 inches or thinner at 0 F or below for at least 30 days against trichinella; handling rules; wild-game cautions; reaching 160 F internally by heating in marinade before drying or in an oven after drying, without case hardening; slices no thicker than 1/4 inch; dry in a dehydrator or oven preheated to 140 F until a test piece cracks but does not break; ground-meat jerky is harder; home-dried jerky keeps 2 weeks at room temperature in a sealed container, longer refrigerated or frozen.
sources.notes: Page text credits "So Easy to Preserve", 6th ed. 2014 (Bulletin 989, UGA Cooperative Extension). No page-level date is shown. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

sources.title: Meat, Ground or Chopped (pressure canning)
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
sources.supports: A tested pressure-canning process for ground or chopped meat: it must be read with Using Pressure Canners; process time varies by jar size, and canner pressure varies by dial-gauge versus weighted-gauge canner and by elevation band (separate tables). The tables are NOT reproduced in the article.
sources.notes: Page text says it was adapted from the Complete Guide to Home Canning, Agriculture Information Bulletin No. 539, USDA, revised 2015. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

sources.title: Keep Your Food Safe During Emergencies: Power Outages, Floods & Fires
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Power-outage planning (appliance thermometers: refrigerator 40 F or below, freezer 0 F or below; group and fill the freezer; cooler and gel packs); refrigerator safe up to 4 hours; full freezer about 48 hours (24 half full); 50 lb dry ice holds an 18 cu ft freezer 2 days; do not put perishable food in snow; never taste food to judge safety; lists of foods to discard after more than 4 hours without power and foods that are safe; frozen-food rules; flood and fire guidance; USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline 1-888-674-6854.
sources.notes: Visible 'Last Updated' is Aug 07, 2013; it is the older, longer FSIS page and the shorter Ask USDA articles point to it. Its bleach sanitizing amounts (1 tablespoon per gallon) differ from CDC's and Ready.gov's.

sources.title: Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Appliance thermometers (refrigerator 40 F or below, freezer 0 F or below); doors closed; food safe up to 4 hours in a refrigerator, 48 hours in a full freezer, 24 hours in a half-full freezer; move perishables to a cooler with a cold source at 4 hours; throw out perishables after 4 hours without power or a cold source; never taste food to judge safety; refreeze or cook thawed food that still has ice crystals or is 40 F or below; flood-food and canned-food steps including its own bleach solution amounts.
sources.notes: Its bleach sanitizing amounts (1 cup per 5 gallons) differ from FSIS and FDA (1 tablespoon per gallon) and Ready.gov (1 part bleach to 10 parts water). Not reproduced in the articles.

sources.title: Food Safety During Power Outage (charts)
sources.publisher: FoodSafety.gov (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services)
sources.supports: Refrigerator keeps food safe up to 4 hours; item-by-item keep-or-discard chart for refrigerated food exposed to 40 F or above for more than 2 hours; item-by-item refreeze-or-discard chart for frozen food (ice crystals versus above 40 F for more than 2 hours); full freezer 48 hours, half full 24; never taste food to judge safety.
sources.notes: Visible 'Date Last Reviewed' is August 8, 2024; page metadata shows a 2024-08-15 modification. The chart's 2-hour column and the 4-hour refrigerator rule are two different clocks that readers often merge.

sources.title: Food and Water Safety During Power Outages and Floods
sources.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
sources.supports: Prepare: appliance thermometers, freeze water containers (melting ice can also supply drinking water), freeze items, group freezer food, coolers, ice, dry or block ice; during: refrigerator about 4 hours, full freezer about 48 hours, 50 lb dry ice holds an 18 cu ft freezer two days; cook meat, poultry, fish, eggs to a safe minimum internal temperature; discard perishables held at room temperature 2 hours or more (1 hour above 90 F); after: refrigerated perishables above 40 F for 4 hours or more should be discarded, and perishables at 45 F or below measured with a food thermometer should be safe but cooked and eaten promptly; foodborne-illness symptoms and timing (20 minutes to 6 weeks); flood food and water steps.
sources.notes: Page metadata shows a 2024-03-05 modification and a 2025-02-25 publication, which look inconsistent; both recorded as shown. The 45 F allowance appears here but not in the FSIS, CDC or Ready.gov pages we read. Its bleach amounts are 1 tablespoon per gallon of 5.25% bleach for utensils and counters but 1 cup in 5 gallons for cans; FSIS uses 1 tablespoon per gallon for cans and CDC 1 cup in 5 gallons throughout.

sources.title: Food
sources.publisher: FEMA / Ready.gov
sources.supports: Store at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food; choose foods your family will eat; special dietary needs; example items including a manual can opener; do not eat from swollen, dented or corroded cans; throw away food at room temperature two hours or more; refrigerator about four hours unopened; discard perishables above 40 F for two hours or more; dry ice 25 lb for a 10 cu ft freezer three to four days, gloves, no direct contact with food; heating canned food and a bleach-to-water disinfecting ratio.
sources.notes: Its dry-ice figure (25 lb, 10 cu ft, three to four days) and its 'two hours or more above 40 F' rule differ in framing from FSIS and FDA. Its can-disinfecting ratio (1 part bleach to 10 parts water) differs from FSIS, FDA and CDC. Newer FEMA material (fact sheet V-1008, December 2023) states the discard rule as 'exposed to temperatures 40 degrees Fahrenheit or higher for more than 4 hours', not two hours; see food-fema-outage-sheet.

sources.title: Shelf-Stable Food Safety
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: What shelf stable means; canned-food shelf-life limits (rust, dents, heat above 100 F; below 85 F best; check the pantry every few weeks and use older cans); discard heavily rusted, deeply dented, swollen, spurting cans; accidentally frozen cans; botulism in canned goods, spores, symptoms in 12 to 48 hours; precautions for home-canned foods (boil low-acid and tomato foods 10 minutes, plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft, not a guarantee); dating is not required and is about quality; can codes are not use-by dates; drying and jerky temperature; home-dried jerky shelf life 1 to 2 months; storage chart.
sources.notes: INTERNAL CONFLICT: its storage chart says home-canned foods keep 12 months and to boil 10 minutes (high-acid) or 20 minutes (low-acid) before using, while its own text says boil low-acid and tomato foods 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft and that properly home-canned fruits never needed the boil. CDC's page agrees with the text, not the chart. Read in full (main content) 2026-10-29.

sources.title: Food Product Dating
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Product dating is not required by federal law except for infant formula; dates indicate quality, not safety; meaning of Best if Used By, Sell-By, Use-By, Freeze-By; foods without spoilage signs are wholesome past the date if handled properly; infant formula Use-By is regulated and formula should not be used after it; can codes are not Best-if-Used-By dates; high-acid canned foods keep best quality 12 to 18 months, low-acid 2 to 5 years; donation after the date; USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline hours.
sources.notes: A can's 'closed' code and an 'open' calendar date are different things on the same can.

sources.title: FoodKeeper App
sources.publisher: FoodSafety.gov (HHS); developed by USDA FSIS with Cornell University and the Food Marketing Institute
sources.supports: The FoodKeeper is a searchable storage-guidance tool, also available as a mobile app, developed by USDA FSIS with Cornell University and the Food Marketing Institute, covering categories including shelf-stable foods.
sources.notes: READ SCOPE: landing text and category list only, not individual entries. No storage durations are taken from it.

sources.title: Room Temperature Storage
sources.publisher: University of Illinois Extension (Food Safety)
sources.supports: Pantry tips (keep storage dry, off the ground, apart from cleaning supplies, cover opened food against pests, do not use swollen cans, rotate first in first out); meaning of package dates including pack dates and expiration dates; points to the USDA FoodKeeper.
sources.notes: No page date shown.

sources.title: Storing Canned Goods
sources.publisher: Utah State University Extension
sources.supports: Commercially canned food is superior to home canned for food storage; label purchase month and year; store cool, dark, dry, off the floor, away from furnaces, pipes and attics; do not let cans or jars freeze; first in first out; discard dented, bulging, rusty or leaky cans; shelf-life general rules; it suggests tasting a sample of older canned food that looks and smells normal.
sources.notes: CONFLICT: its suggestion to taste a sample and its boiling advice for older canned food (heat low-acid food to 165 F or boil 5 to 10 minutes) differ from CDC and FSIS ('never taste', boil 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft). No page date shown; references run to 2006.

sources.title: Survival Basics: Food - How to Stock Up and Prepare for Natural Disasters (EM 9331)
sources.publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service
sources.supports: Eat refrigerated food first, then frozen, then pantry; store food your family will eat so you can cycle through it; add a little each shop and use sales; inspect stored food for pests every six months with a calendar alert; storage locations and small-home tips; two-week and four-week targets are Oregon planning figures; after the refrigerator passes 40 F most refrigerated foods keep no longer than two more hours; home-canning cautions including that vacuum-sealing low-acid foods stored at room temperature can create an environment for botulism toxin; do not can water, butter, dairy, grains, leftovers, cakes, quick breads or cured meats.
sources.notes: Written for the Cascadia earthquake scenario; the 2-week and 4-week supply targets are Oregon-specific. The 'updated' date is page metadata. It says eggs can be kept at room temperature up to six days unless washed or cooked, which most store eggs have been; we do not repeat it.

sources.title: Jerky and Food Safety
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Pathogenic bacteria are likely to survive dry heat and the 130 to 140 F of a food dehydrator; Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7 illnesses from homemade jerky; USDA Hotline recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating, then dry at a constant 130 to 140 F; why the order matters (evaporation keeps the meat cool, bacteria become more heat resistant); sun drying not recommended; summary of a 2004 Journal of Food Protection study (marination alone did not reduce the pathogen; E. coli survived up to 10 hours at up to 145 F in lab-inoculated venison) and a 1998 study on ground beef jerky with and without a nitrite curing mix; wild-game contamination; storage times (commercial 12 months, home-dried 1 to 2 months).
sources.notes: Studies are reported as FSIS summarizes them; we did not read the journal articles. Currency check 2026-10-30 in a browser: the page still shows 'Last Updated: Nov 03, 2016' and the same 160 F / 165 F, 130 to 140 F and 1 to 2 months figures as the newer Ask USDA article (Feb 2025). Kansas State MF3173 cites an FSIS 'Jerky and Food Safety' fact sheet dated September 22, 2023 at a /meat/jerky path; we could not retrieve that version (automated fetch refused), so we cannot say whether it differs.

sources.title: How can I make meat or poultry jerky at home?
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
sources.supports: Current USDA Hotline recommendation: heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating (steam or roast, checked with a food thermometer); dehydrator with an adjustable temperature dial that holds 130 to 140 F throughout drying; dry until a test piece cracks but does not break; 10 to 24 hours when not heated in marinade; seven handling steps.
sources.notes: Newer than the longer FSIS fact sheet (2016 date) and consistent with it.

sources.title: Dehydrating Meat Safely at Home (MF3173)
sources.publisher: Kansas State University Research and Extension
sources.supports: USDA recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F; a dehydrator may not reach those temperatures; keep dehydrator at 130 to 140 F and do not raise it to rush drying because higher heat causes case hardening; the two NCHFP heating methods; ground-meat jerky needs 160 F, heat 10 minutes in an oven after dehydrating; raw poultry not recommended for jerky for texture and flavor; homemade jerky best used within 1 to 2 months, refrigerate or freeze for longer.
sources.notes: Revised March 2026 per the publication. Cites the NCHFP, FSIS and NDSU pages. Its 1-to-2-month storage figure agrees with FSIS and disagrees with NCHFP's 2 weeks.

sources.title: Using Pressure Canners
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (Andress, rev. 2014)
sources.supports: Dial versus weighted gauges; UL-approved canners only; a canner should hold at least 4 quart jars to be a pressure canner for USDA processes; serious errors from not adjusting for elevation, air trapped in the canner (vent 10 minutes before pressurizing) and an inaccurate dial gauge (check yearly; replace if off by more than 2 pounds at 5, 10 or 15 pounds); step-by-step operation; if pressure drops, restart the full timing; do not force-cool; jars sit 12 to 24 hours; burner cautions.
sources.notes: This page says the canner pressurizes 'during the next 3 to 10 minutes'; the NCHFP 'How to Use Boiling Water and Pressure Canners' page says 3 to 5. Minor, but recorded.

sources.title: Ensuring Safe Canned Foods
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, rev. 2015)
sources.supports: Botulism growth conditions (moist low-acid food, 40 to 120 F, under 2 percent oxygen, toxin in 3 to 4 days); spores harmless on fresh food because they need an airless environment; low-acid foods have pH above 4.6 and include red meats, seafood, poultry, milk and all fresh vegetables except most tomatoes; low-acid foods must be sterilized at 240 to 250 F in pressure canners at 10 to 15 PSIG; the time range for low-acid food in a boiling-water canner is 7 to 11 hours; use the recommended research-based times; altitude of 1,000 ft or more needs adjusted processes; store below 95 F (50 to 70 F for quality).
sources.notes: Washing fresh food reduces microorganisms only slightly; peeling and blanching help; method and tested times are the vital controls.

sources.title: How to Use Boiling Water and Pressure Canners
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
sources.supports: Low-acid foods must be processed in a pressure canner to be free of botulism risks; pressure does not destroy microorganisms, temperature held long enough does; at sea level 10.5 lb gauge pressure gives 240 F; elevation and trapped air are the two serious errors; venting; weighted-gauge limits above 1,000 ft; dial gauges checked each year, counties' Cooperative Extension offices may test them; pressure saucepans with smaller capacity are not recommended; the 10-step pressure-canner routine.
sources.notes: Page text says it was adapted from the Complete Guide, 'revised 2009'. It says the canner pressurizes in 3 to 5 minutes; the NCHFP 'Using Pressure Canners' page says 3 to 10.

sources.title: Canning in Electric Multi-Cookers (Newsflash)
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia
sources.supports: NCHFP does not support the use of USDA canning processes in electric multi-cooker appliances, even those with canning or steam-canning buttons, and gives four reasons: no thermal-process work with jars inside them, temperature (not pressure) is what matters, temperature must stay at minimum through the process, and USDA low-acid processes count heat from coming up to pressure and from natural cooling.
sources.notes: Dated February 1, 2019. Excludes the Ball electric boiling-water-style canner for acid foods.

sources.title: Dry Canning Raw Vegetables is an Unsafe Practice
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia
sources.supports: Pressure canning raw vegetables in jars with no added liquid is potentially very hazardous; the covering liquid is required for heat penetration; bacteria die more slowly in dry heat; butter or ghee are no substitute; botulism toxin may be present with no visible or odor change; research-based processes must be used as written, including altitude adjustments.
sources.notes: A blog post, not a regulation, but from the NCHFP and referring to the USDA hotline calls it was prompted by.

sources.title: Equipment and Methods Not Recommended (Canning)
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
sources.supports: Open-kettle canning and processing filled jars in conventional ovens, microwave ovens and dishwashers are not recommended; canning powders are useless as preservatives; pressure above 15 PSI not recommended for new equipment; 'dry canning' of vegetables without covering liquid and 'dry canning' of dry foods by heating jars in an oven are not recommended; steam canners are described as not currently recommended, with a pointer to newer atmospheric steam-canner guidance.
sources.notes: STALE-TEXT NOTE: this page still says steam canners are not currently recommended, while a September 2026 NCHFP newsflash calls atmospheric steam canning safe for high-acid foods when tested recipes and steps are followed. Neither concerns low-acid foods.

sources.title: Atmospheric Steam Canning Statement (Newsflash)
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia
sources.supports: NCHFP considers atmospheric steam canning a safe method for high-acid foods (fruits, jams, pickles, tomatoes) when tested recipes and guidelines are followed; it says nothing that extends this to low-acid foods.
sources.notes: Dated 'September 2026' on the page. The URL slug contains a typo ('tatement') and is reproduced as is.

sources.title: Home-Canned Foods (Botulism Prevention)
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Follow the USDA Complete Guide; do not use other recipes even from a trusted friend or relative; low-acid foods (pH above 4.6) are the most common source of home-canning botulism and home-canned vegetables the most common cause of US outbreaks; pressure canning is the only recommended method for low-acid foods; do not use a boiling water canner or an electric multi-cooker for them; use a canner that holds at least four 1-quart jars upright, an accurate gauge (county extension offices often check gauges), vented before pressurizing; use current processing times for old recipes; can only a year's worth; store 50 to 70 F for quality, never above 95 F; boil home-canned low-acid foods and tomatoes 10 minutes plus 1 minute per additional 1,000 ft before eating; signs of contamination; if in doubt, throw it out.
sources.notes: Page lists 'Published May 15, 2024' and 'Updated April 25, 2024', which is the order CDC shows; recorded as shown.

sources.title: Guide 1: Principles of Home Canning (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, rev. 2015)
sources.publisher: USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture, hosted by NCHFP
sources.supports: Storage of canned food (clean, cool, dark, dry; not above 95 F or near heat sources or in direct sunlight); accidental freezing does not by itself cause spoilage unless jars unseal; identifying spoilage (check seals, bubbles, odors, spurting liquid, mold); spoiled low-acid foods may show little evidence and should be treated as having produced botulinum toxin, with sealed suspects double-bagged for the trash and unsealed ones detoxified before disposal; contact with the toxin can be fatal whether ingested or through the skin.
sources.notes: A 40-page PDF. READ SCOPE: the extracted text was searched and read only in these sections: 'Ensuring safe canned foods' (incl. the 95 F figure), 'Equipment and methods not recommended', 'Reprocessing unsealed jars', 'Storing canned foods' and 'Identifying and handling spoiled canned food' (the cleanup paragraph was read only up to the start of the bleach-solution sentence). The rest was NOT read. Detoxification steps are not reproduced in the articles. Kind changed to regulator because the publisher is a USDA agency; it is hosted by a university.

sources.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008)
sources.publisher: FEMA / Ready.gov
sources.supports: Keep freezers and refrigerators closed; a refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours and a full freezer stays at a safe temperature for about 48 hours; do not store food outside or in snow; keep a thermometer in the refrigerator and freezer; throw away refrigerated food exposed to 40 F or higher for more than 4 hours, and food with an unusual odor, color or texture; make a plan with your doctor for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more unless the drug's label says otherwise, call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medication that has been at room temperature, and use the medicine only until you have a new supply; use generators outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings.
sources.notes: READ SCOPE: the whole one-page sheet, read as text extracted with pdftotext from a local copy of the PDF fetched 2026-10-30 (Firecrawl and the web-fetch tool could not extract it; Firecrawl was out of credits). Document code and date read from the sheet itself: 'FEMA V-1008/December 2023'. This is newer than the Ready.gov Food page's 'two hours' framing, and it is the document used for the medication line. We did not read the older 2020 FEMA wording the lead mentioned.

sources.title: People at Increased Risk for Food Poisoning
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Higher-risk groups for severe food poisoning: people 65 and older, children under 5, people with weakened immune systems (examples listed), and pregnant women; it is especially important for them to take steps to prevent food poisoning; it points to separate 'Safer Food Choices' pages for each group.
sources.notes: READ SCOPE: the whole page, read in a browser pane on 2026-10-30. One date shown (Jan. 31, 2025), not labelled published, updated or reviewed. The four 'Safer Food Choices' pages it links were NOT read, so no food-specific advice for these groups is taken from this source.
